systemPrompt:
You are an expert at planning interactive 3D visualizations for textbook figures.

PRIMARY CONTEXT:
The generated figure will be embedded alongside the original in a PDF reader. It should look recognizably like the source figure — same general geometry, viewpoint, labels, and proportions — but does not need to be a pixel-perfect inline replacement. Some additional controls or layout breathing room are fine if they genuinely help the learner.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY valid JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "projection_type": "perspective | axonometric | oblique",
  "camera_view": { "azimuthDeg": <perspective only — 0=side · 45=three-quarter · 90=front-on>, "elevationDeg": <perspective only — 0=eye-level · 20-35=slightly above · 90=top-down>, "rollDeg": 0, "heightFraction": <0.5 default · up to 0.75 to fill the frame> },
  "axis_screen_angles": <axonometric only — null for a flat 2D plot/diagram with no 3D depth (front-on view); omit this field entirely for a 3D axonometric figure (renderer uses a standard isometric pose)>,
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every geometric element visible in the figure that must be recreated in 3D"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "uniqueCamelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields — see INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "geometry_notes": "Approximate world-space scale (e.g. 'cube ~2 units side, axes span ±3'), dominant colors from the source, and any domain-specific formula or value needed for correctness.",
  "notes": "Three.js / rendering technique notes (distinct from geometry_notes)"
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

Rules:
- PROJECTION TYPE: pick whichever the source most resembles. Do not measure angles off the image — the renderer applies a fixed standard pose for each type, so a coarse visual call is enough. Spend your effort on ELEMENTS and INTERACTIONS instead; camera is a quick classification, not a measurement task.
  • "perspective" — depth edges clearly converge toward a vanishing point, or a single object's own far end reads smaller than its near end. Judge within one object; a row of separate same-shape objects that merely shrink (e.g. neural-net layers) is not perspective.
  • "oblique" — one face is drawn true (an undistorted rectangle: right angles, horizontal/vertical edges intact) while depth recedes off it along a single diagonal — e.g. stacked feature maps/filter banks drawn as offset same-size copies.
  • "axonometric" — the default for everything else: any other 3D-looking figure (axes tilted, no true face), or a flat 2D plot/diagram (set "axis_screen_angles": null for these).
- CAMERA VIEW: camera_view sets framing only. azimuthDeg/elevationDeg apply to perspective only: azimuthDeg 0 side, 45 three-quarter, 90 front-on; elevationDeg 0 eye-level, 10–20 low-angle, 25–35 moderate three-quarter, 90 top-down. rollDeg is usually 0. heightFraction is how much of the frame the figure should fill (0.5 default, up to 0.75).
- DEMO STEPS: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases the learner should visit in sequence, each step driving one named configuration of the interaction state. Use [] for a single continuous exploration with no natural sequence.
- GEOMETRY NOTES: always fill this in — it is what stops the generator guessing sizes and getting the zoom wrong. Cover:
  • world-space dimensions, and for oblique/axonometric figures give each box explicitly as X × Y × Z world units, naming which source dimension each axis carries (+X is screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z the receding diagonal).
  • the colour palette, with hex codes where determinable from the source.
  • any formula or numeric range the generator needs to be mathematically correct.
  • POSITION AND ORIENTATION for each element as read off the source — which way it points, what angle it sits at, which side of another element it is on. Read this off the image; do not infer layout from general knowledge of the concept. A generic, plausible-looking arrangement is the failure mode the generator falls into whenever geometry_notes covers only dimensions.
  • for a repeated shape with a stated per-element value (channel count, layer size, category), an explicit number for each element's varying dimension tied to that value — equal values get equal size, even across sequence position — rather than a described trend.
- MULTI-PART FIGURES: if the source contains multiple labeled panels ((a)/(b)/(c), side-by-side comparisons, before/after pairs, sequential diagrams), do NOT recreate them all simultaneously in the initial view. Show one panel by default and link the rest through a single interaction — a toggle, tab, or slider — so the learner actively moves between parts. The transition itself should teach the comparison or progression.
- Prefer interactions that expose relationships in the figure rather than generic controls.

Figure: CNX_Chem_08_04_Gouy

AUTHOR-PROVIDED INTERACTION REQUESTS:
Requested interactions:
- Toggle between a paramagnetic sample and a diamagnetic sample: watch the balance tip toward the magnet or away from it and update the sign of the magnetic susceptibility
- Slider for magnetic field strength: observe proportional deflection of the balance arm and read off the corresponding susceptibility value
- Animate the weighing procedure: show the sample tube being drawn into or repelled from the magnetic field region as the electromagnets energize

Source file:
OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 8

Use these requested interactions when forming the plan. Use the image to recover visual structure, layout, labels, camera/view cues, and missing visible elements.

Planner context:
This figure illustrates a Gouy balance apparatus used to measure magnetic susceptibility, showing a vertically suspended sample tube positioned between two cylindrical electromagnets and counterbalanced on a traditional beam balance against calibrated reference weights. The sample tube, labeled "Sample," hangs from one arm of the balance beam down into the gap between the two poles labeled "Electromagnets," while the opposite arm holds a pan carrying calibrated masses; the label "Magnetic field" with a line points to the region inside the gap, where curved purple arrows radiate outward in concentric arcs representing the inhomogeneous field lines diverging from the magnet poles. Because a paramagnetic sample containing unpaired electrons is drawn into the stronger-field region of the gap, it experiences a net downward force that makes it appear heavier, shifting the beam, while a diamagnetic sample with all electrons paired is weakly repelled and appears slightly lighter. The change in apparent mass — measured by adding or removing calibrated weights until the beam re-levels — is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, providing a direct experimental count of those electrons. This figure introduces the Gouy balance as the key instrument for determining magnetic susceptibility and motivates its use to reveal that O2 possesses two unpaired electrons, a fact the Lewis-structure model fails to predict.

CONTEXT FROM TEXTBOOK:

The sample tube, labeled "Sample," hangs from one arm of the balance beam down into the gap between the two poles labeled "Electromagnets," while the opposite arm holds a pan carrying calibrated masses; the label "Magnetic field" with a line points to the region inside the gap, where curved purple arrows radiate outward in concentric arcs representing the inhomogeneous field lines diverging from the magnet poles. Because a paramagnetic sample containing unpaired electrons is drawn into the stronger-field region of the gap, it experiences a net downward force that makes it appear heavier, shifting the beam, while a diamagnetic sample with all electrons paired is weakly repelled and appears slightly lighter. The change in apparent mass — measured by adding or removing calibrated weights until the beam re-levels — is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, providing a direct experimental count of those electrons. This figure introduces the Gouy balance as the key instrument for determining magnetic susceptibility and motivates its use to reveal that O2 possesses two unpaired electrons, a fact the Lewis-structure model fails to predict.

PROJECTION TYPE: perspective
Use the scaffold's true perspective projection after building all geometry. Use this only when the source has real vanishing-point convergence or distance-based size shrinkage; then depth should visibly affect apparent size.

ELEMENTS TO RECREATE IN 3D:
  - brass-colored circular base plate (flat disc, elliptical in view) at bottom right of scene
  - vertical brass support column rising from base center
  - pointed fulcrum tip at top of column supporting the beam
  - horizontal brass balance beam with rounded up-curled hooks at both ends, pivoting on the fulcrum
  - thin black suspension wire from the LEFT hook down to the sample tube
  - glass sample tube (thin cylinder with rounded bottom and flared lip/collar at top) hanging vertically on the left
  - blue liquid/solid sample filling the lower two-thirds of the tube
  - left cylindrical electromagnet pole piece (horizontal cylinder, visible elliptical face toward the gap)
  - right cylindrical electromagnet pole piece (mirror of the left, same size)
  - narrow gap between the two pole faces, with the sample tube passing vertically through it
  - purple curved magnetic field lines: dense concentric arcs filling the gap around the tube plus arrows fanning outward above, below and to the sides of each pole
  - small arrowheads on every field line indicating direction into the poles
  - four black cords from the RIGHT hook down to a shallow brass weighing pan
  - shallow brass weighing pan (ellipse with rim) on the right
  - three small silver calibrated cylindrical weights sitting in the pan
  - text label 'Sample' with leader line to the tube
  - text label 'Magnetic field' with leader line to a field arc above the gap
  - text label 'Electromagnets' with a two-branch leader pointing to both pole cylinders
  - readout panel showing magnetic susceptibility sign/value and apparent mass change

GEOMETRY NOTES (world-space scale, color palette, and any formula/value needed for correctness — build to these so sizes, zoom, and colors match the source; do not guess dimensions the notes already specify):
World units: whole apparatus ~7 wide × 5 tall. Stand sits RIGHT of center: base disc center (1.2, 0, 0), radius 1.3, thickness 0.18, brass. Vertical column at x=1.2, radius 0.12, from y=0.18 to y=4.3, topped by a small pointed fulcrum (cone, height 0.2) at y=4.3. Balance beam is a slender brass bar of thickness 0.10 running along X from x=-2.4 to x=+3.0 at y=4.45, pivoting about the fulcrum at x=1.2 (so the sample arm is the LONGER left arm, matching the source); both ends finish in up-curled circular hooks of radius 0.14. Beam tilt = clamp(k·χ·B²), max ±8°, positive (left end down) for paramagnetic. LEFT arm: single black wire (radius 0.015) from hook at (-2.4, 4.45) straight down to the tube lip at y=3.25. Sample tube: vertical glass cylinder at x=-2.4, outer radius 0.20, from y=1.05 (hemispherical bottom) to y=3.25, with a flared lip ring (radius 0.28, height 0.10) at the top; blue sample fills from y=1.05 up to y=2.75. ELECTROMAGNETS: two horizontal cylinders with axes along X, radius 0.62, length 0.95 each, centers at (-3.35, 1.95, 0) and (-1.45, 1.95, 0); their inner circular faces are 0.50 apart, so the tube passes exactly through the mid-gap at x=-2.4, y=1.95. Each cylinder is drawn with a visible seam ring 0.25 in from the inner face. RIGHT arm: four black cords from hook at (3.0, 4.45) splaying to the rim of a shallow brass pan centered (3.0, 2.85, 0), pan outer radius 0.70, depth 0.15; three silver weights (cylinders radius 0.13, height 0.26) standing in the pan. FIELD LINES: purple arcs in the XY plane centered on the gap midpoint (-2.4, 1.95); 5-6 nested arcs of semi-major radius 0.45 → 1.9 forming a dipole-like flux pattern that leaves the top and bottom of the gap and curls back to the outer faces of both poles, plus short arrowed segments fanning above, below, left and right of each pole; all arrowheads point INTO the pole pieces. Colors: brass/gold #E3D14B with darker edge #B9A32C and highlight #F5E98A; magnets grey vertical gradient #F0F0F0→#9A9A9A with black outline #000; glass tube pale cyan #D7ECEF at 35% opacity; sample liquid blue #5B7FE0 with lighter top #8FA8F0; weights silver #C9CBCE; field lines purple #8A4FD8; labels black 16px sans with 1.5px black leader lines. Physics: apparent force F = (χ A B²)/(2μ0); use χ_para = +1.8×10⁻³ and χ_dia = −2.5×10⁻⁵ (display sign prominently); apparent Δm displayed in mg scaling as B², e.g. +42 mg at 0.8 T for the paramagnetic sample, −0.6 mg for the diamagnetic one.

DISCRETE CONTROLS (implement every one of these in #ui, each must work independently):
[
  {
    "id": "sampleType",
    "type": "toggle",
    "teaches": "A paramagnetic sample (unpaired electrons) is pulled into the high-field gap so the beam dips on the sample side and χ > 0; a diamagnetic sample (all electrons paired) is weakly pushed out, the beam rises slightly and χ < 0.",
    "label": "Sample",
    "options": [
      "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)",
      "Diamagnetic (all paired)"
    ],
    "default": "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)"
  },
  {
    "id": "fieldStrength",
    "type": "slider",
    "teaches": "The apparent weight change, and therefore the beam deflection, grows with field strength (F ∝ χB²), while the measured susceptibility χ itself stays constant — it is a property of the sample, not of the magnet.",
    "label": "Electromagnet field B (T)",
    "range": [
      0,
      1.5,
      0.05
    ],
    "default": 0.8
  },
  {
    "id": "weighingRun",
    "type": "animation",
    "teaches": "The full measurement: with the magnet off the beam is level, energizing the magnet draws the tube down into (or nudges it out of) the gap, and calibrated weights are added until the beam re-levels — the added mass gives the apparent mass change.",
    "label": "Run weighing procedure",
    "loop": false
  },
  {
    "id": "orbitView",
    "type": "orbit",
    "teaches": "Seeing the apparatus from other angles reveals that the pole pieces are round cylinders facing each other and the tube hangs on the axis of the narrow gap where the field is strongest and most inhomogeneous."
  }
]

DEMO STEPS (tween through these using goToStep(); each step drives the controls above):
[
  {
    "title": "Magnet off — beam level",
    "narration": "With no current in the electromagnets the tube hangs freely in the gap and the beam balances against the calibrated weights. χ cannot yet be read.",
    "state": {
      "fieldStrength": 0,
      "sampleType": "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Energize the magnet — paramagnetic pull",
    "narration": "At 0.8 T the paramagnetic sample is drawn down into the strongest part of the inhomogeneous field; the sample arm dips and the sample appears heavier (χ > 0).",
    "state": {
      "fieldStrength": 0.8,
      "sampleType": "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Stronger field, larger deflection",
    "narration": "Raising B to 1.5 T increases the downward force roughly as B², so the beam tips further — but the susceptibility extracted from it is unchanged.",
    "state": {
      "fieldStrength": 1.5,
      "sampleType": "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Swap in a diamagnetic sample",
    "narration": "With all electrons paired the sample is weakly expelled from the field: the sample arm rises slightly, the apparent mass decreases, and χ is small and negative.",
    "state": {
      "fieldStrength": 1.5,
      "sampleType": "Diamagnetic (all paired)"
    }
  },
  {
    "title": "Re-level with calibrated weights",
    "narration": "Weights are added or removed until the beam is level again; the mass difference is proportional to χ and hence to the number of unpaired electrons.",
    "state": {
      "fieldStrength": 0.8,
      "sampleType": "Paramagnetic (unpaired e⁻)"
    }
  }
]

CAMERA VIEW (framing only). Call setCameraView({ projection, ...these }) AFTER all geometry is added. Keep the projection MECHANISM from PROJECTION TYPE above (orthographic / sheared-oblique / perspective). For perspective these params set the pose (azimuth/elevation/roll); for the two parallel projections pose is a standard default (see PROJECTION TYPE above), and these params set only roll and framing (heightFraction):
{
  "azimuthDeg": 20,
  "elevationDeg": 12,
  "rollDeg": 0,
  "heightFraction": 0.72
}

NOTES: Build the beam, wire, tube and pan as one pivot Group rotated about the fulcrum on Z so all suspended parts swing together; keep the tube and pan hanging vertically by counter-rotating them (or suspend them from pivot points) so they stay plumb as the beam tilts. Magnet cylinders: CylinderGeometry rotated π/2 about Z, MeshStandardMaterial with a canvas gradient map for the metallic banding plus EdgesGeometry black outline to match the flat illustrative style. Field lines: TubeGeometry along CatmullRomCurve3 arcs (or thick Line2 from three/examples) in #8A4FD8; arrowheads as small ConeGeometry instances placed along each curve; fade line opacity and shrink arc count linearly with the fieldStrength slider (fully hidden at B=0). Glass tube: MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission 0.8, roughness 0.1, depthWrite false, rendered last. Labels as CSS2DRenderer divs anchored to the tube, a field arc, and both magnets, with SVG/Line leader lines drawn in the same overlay. Animation timeline (~6 s): level → field ramps up with field lines fading in → tube visibly pulled ~0.05 units down/up and beam tilts with slight damped oscillation → weights drop into the pan one by one → beam returns to level. Use lights: hemisphere + one directional key from upper left to mimic the flat textbook shading; white background.

Follow the interaction plan above.

systemPrompt:
You are an expert at planning interactive 3D visualizations for textbook figures.

PRIMARY CONTEXT:
The generated figure will be embedded alongside the original in a PDF reader. It should look recognizably like the source figure — same general geometry, viewpoint, labels, and proportions — but does not need to be a pixel-perfect inline replacement. Some additional controls or layout breathing room are fine if they genuinely help the learner.

INTERACTION PALETTE — choose the interactions that best fit the concept. Pick the fewest that genuinely serve the learning goal; more is not better. In "teaches", say what the learner understands, not what the control does.

• orbit / drag — rotate/move the scene. When depth or 3D shape IS the concept.
• hover — reveal a label on demand. When showing every label at once clutters.
• click — highlight one element. When focus on one part of a busy scene matters.
• slider — sweep one continuous variable. When dragging it visibly transforms the figure.
• toggle — switch between 2+ named views. For before/after or dual views (e.g. spatial ↔ frequency).
• button / state — step through discrete phases. When distinct stages should be visited deliberately.
• animation — self-playing motion. When the concept is inherently dynamic and a slider can't convey it.
• equation_input — learner types math, parsed at runtime. When "change the formula, reshape the output" (integrand, boundary, kernel); each field maps to one curve/quantity; catch parse errors inline.
• code_editor — learner writes/debugs an algorithm; the figure replays its execution frame by frame. Use ONLY when the concept IS a procedure whose intermediate states carry the lesson — heapify, one pass of a sort, a graph traversal, gradient descent, scanline fill — i.e. the question a learner has is "in what order does it touch the data, and why". Needs state small enough to draw whole (~30 elements) and an algorithm expressible in ~20 lines against a handful of operations. Do NOT use it for a continuous parameter (that is a slider), a formula the learner retypes (equation_input), or a static structure with no execution (hover/click). Choose it over animation when the learner should be able to get the procedure WRONG and watch where it diverges.

Output ONLY valid JSON (no markdown, no explanation):
{
  "projection_type": "perspective | axonometric | oblique",
  "camera_view": { "azimuthDeg": <perspective only — 0=side · 45=three-quarter · 90=front-on>, "elevationDeg": <perspective only — 0=eye-level · 20-35=slightly above · 90=top-down>, "rollDeg": 0, "heightFraction": <0.5 default · up to 0.75 to fill the frame> },
  "axis_screen_angles": <axonometric only — null for a flat 2D plot/diagram with no 3D depth (front-on view); omit this field entirely for a 3D axonometric figure (renderer uses a standard isometric pose)>,
  "elements": ["exhaustive list of every geometric element visible in the figure that must be recreated in 3D"],
  "interactions": [
    { "id": "uniqueCamelCaseId", "type": "orbit | drag | hover | click | slider | toggle | button | state | animation | equation_input | code_editor", "teaches": "what the learner understands", "...": "plus ONLY that type's fields — see INTERACTION FIELDS below" }
  ],
  "demo_steps": [
    {
      "title": "Step name shown in UI",
      "narration": "What the learner sees and understands at this step — one or two sentences",
      "state": { "interactionId": value }
    }
  ],
  "geometry_notes": "Approximate world-space scale (e.g. 'cube ~2 units side, axes span ±3'), dominant colors from the source, and any domain-specific formula or value needed for correctness.",
  "notes": "Three.js / rendering technique notes (distinct from geometry_notes)"
}

INTERACTION FIELDS — every interaction object has "id" (unique camelCase), "type", and "teaches". Add ONLY the fields listed for its type; never attach a "range" to anything but a slider.

"type" MUST be exactly one of these 11 strings: "orbit" · "drag" · "hover" · "click" · "slider" · "toggle" · "button" · "state" · "animation" · "equation_input" · "code_editor""

• orbit / drag / hover / click — no extra fields.
• animation      — "label", optional "loop": true | false.
• slider         — "label", "range": [min, max, step], "default": <number>.
• toggle         — "label", "options": ["A", "B", ...], "default": "A"   (a plain on/off toggle may drop "options" and use "default": true | false).
• button / state — "label", "states": ["idle", "running", "done"], "default": "idle".
• equation_input — "label", "fields": [ { "id": "...", "label": "f(x) =", "default": "sin(x)", "variables": ["x"], "domain": [min, max], "role": "integrand | boundary | kernel | ..." } ]. "domain" is the x-range the field is plotted over; always supply it so the generator does not have to guess.
• code_editor    — "label",
                   "entry_point": "the one function the learner must define, e.g. buildMaxHeap(heap)",
                   "api": [ { "op": "greater(i, j)", "does": "true when A[i] > A[j]" }, { "op": "swap(i, j)", "does": "exchange two elements — the ONLY way to mutate" }, ... ],
                   "frame": "what one recorded step shows, e.g. 'the whole array plus the 1-2 indices the op touched'",
                   "input": { "label": "Initial array", "default": "4, 1, 3, 2, 16, 9, 10" },
                   "sample_code": "<correct implementation, as a string>",
                   optional "buggy_code": "<plausible near-miss, with a comment naming the bug>",
                   "success_check": "the property the final state must satisfy, e.g. 'every parent >= both of its children'".
  Design the "api" first and keep it minimal: 4–7 ops covering read, compare, mutate, and annotate (a note/mark op for the learner's own commentary). Every state change must be reachable ONLY through an op — otherwise the replay has gaps. The learner writes algorithm logic, never drawing code.

demo_steps "state" may set values for slider, toggle, and button/state interactions only; code_editor and equation_input are seeded by their sample_code / fields defaults, not by demo_steps.

Rules:
- PROJECTION TYPE: pick whichever the source most resembles. Do not measure angles off the image — the renderer applies a fixed standard pose for each type, so a coarse visual call is enough. Spend your effort on ELEMENTS and INTERACTIONS instead; camera is a quick classification, not a measurement task.
  • "perspective" — depth edges clearly converge toward a vanishing point, or a single object's own far end reads smaller than its near end. Judge within one object; a row of separate same-shape objects that merely shrink (e.g. neural-net layers) is not perspective.
  • "oblique" — one face is drawn true (an undistorted rectangle: right angles, horizontal/vertical edges intact) while depth recedes off it along a single diagonal — e.g. stacked feature maps/filter banks drawn as offset same-size copies.
  • "axonometric" — the default for everything else: any other 3D-looking figure (axes tilted, no true face), or a flat 2D plot/diagram (set "axis_screen_angles": null for these).
- CAMERA VIEW: camera_view sets framing only. azimuthDeg/elevationDeg apply to perspective only: azimuthDeg 0 side, 45 three-quarter, 90 front-on; elevationDeg 0 eye-level, 10–20 low-angle, 25–35 moderate three-quarter, 90 top-down. rollDeg is usually 0. heightFraction is how much of the frame the figure should fill (0.5 default, up to 0.75).
- DEMO STEPS: include when the concept has 2+ distinct phases the learner should visit in sequence, each step driving one named configuration of the interaction state. Use [] for a single continuous exploration with no natural sequence.
- GEOMETRY NOTES: always fill this in — it is what stops the generator guessing sizes and getting the zoom wrong. Cover:
  • world-space dimensions, and for oblique/axonometric figures give each box explicitly as X × Y × Z world units, naming which source dimension each axis carries (+X is screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z the receding diagonal).
  • the colour palette, with hex codes where determinable from the source.
  • any formula or numeric range the generator needs to be mathematically correct.
  • POSITION AND ORIENTATION for each element as read off the source — which way it points, what angle it sits at, which side of another element it is on. Read this off the image; do not infer layout from general knowledge of the concept. A generic, plausible-looking arrangement is the failure mode the generator falls into whenever geometry_notes covers only dimensions.
  • for a repeated shape with a stated per-element value (channel count, layer size, category), an explicit number for each element's varying dimension tied to that value — equal values get equal size, even across sequence position — rather than a described trend.
- MULTI-PART FIGURES: if the source contains multiple labeled panels ((a)/(b)/(c), side-by-side comparisons, before/after pairs, sequential diagrams), do NOT recreate them all simultaneously in the initial view. Show one panel by default and link the rest through a single interaction — a toggle, tab, or slider — so the learner actively moves between parts. The transition itself should teach the comparison or progression.
- Prefer interactions that expose relationships in the figure rather than generic controls.

Figure: CNX_Chem_08_04_Gouy

Context:
This figure illustrates a Gouy balance apparatus used to measure magnetic susceptibility, showing a vertically suspended sample tube positioned between two cylindrical electromagnets and counterbalanced on a traditional beam balance against calibrated reference weights. The sample tube, labeled "Sample," hangs from one arm of the balance beam down into the gap between the two poles labeled "Electromagnets," while the opposite arm holds a pan carrying calibrated masses; the label "Magnetic field" with a line points to the region inside the gap, where curved purple arrows radiate outward in concentric arcs representing the inhomogeneous field lines diverging from the magnet poles. Because a paramagnetic sample containing unpaired electrons is drawn into the stronger-field region of the gap, it experiences a net downward force that makes it appear heavier, shifting the beam, while a diamagnetic sample with all electrons paired is weakly repelled and appears slightly lighter. The change in apparent mass — measured by adding or removing calibrated weights until the beam re-levels — is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, providing a direct experimental count of those electrons. This figure introduces the Gouy balance as the key instrument for determining magnetic susceptibility and motivates its use to reveal that O2 possesses two unpaired electrons, a fact the Lewis-structure model fails to predict.
